Stock and flow side by side, with the decomposition

Source: R/custody.R
stkflow.Rd

Reports the same person-days as a stock and as a flow, and says how much of any change in the stock came from the number of people and how much from how long they stayed. Use it whenever a report compares periods: the count of people (a flow) and the population held (a stock) can move in opposite directions when the length of stay changes, and a table with only one of them implies the wrong direction for the other.

Usage

stkflow(
  days,
  people,
  prd = NULL,
  t = 365,
  expo = NULL,
  per = 1e+05,
  base = c("first", "previous")
)

Arguments

days

Numeric vector of person-days, one element per period; non-negative, no NA or Inf.

people

Numeric vector of the number of people (admissions or persons served), one element per period, the same length as days; positive.

prd

Optional labels for the periods (any vector, converted to character), one per period. Default NULL labels them 1, 2, ....

t

Numeric, the length of each period in days: one value for all periods, or one per period; positive. Default 365. perdays() turns dates into this.

expo

Optional numeric population to express rates against, one value or one per period, positive; for example provincial residents. Default NULL (no rate columns).

per

Numeric scalar, the rate base when expo is given: rates are per per residents. Default 100000.

base

Character scalar, what the change columns compare against: "first" (the default) measures every period against the first, which is what a report on a whole window wants; "previous" measures each period against the one before it, which is what a series wants (the first row's changes are then NA).

Value

A data frame of class c("rmbl_stock_flow", "data.frame"), one row per period, with columns period (character), people, days, alos (days per person), adp (days divided by t); when exposure is given also exposure, flowrate (people per per residents) and stkrate (adp per per residents). Then the percentage changes against the baseline: peochg, aloschg, dayschg, adpchg, and with exposure also flowratechg and stkratechg. Attribute "stkflow" is a list with t (the period lengths), baseline and per (NA without exposure). The print method shows the levels and a footer with the change from the baseline to the last period, flagging rates with opposite signs.

Details

The decomposition is exact, because days are people times length of stay: a change in days is \((1+p)(1+l) - 1\) for proportional changes \(p\) in people and \(l\) in stay. The two rates can therefore carry OPPOSITE signs, and the point of putting them in one table is that neither can then be quoted alone.

Changes are percentages: \(100 (v_i / v_b - 1)\) with \(b\) the baseline row. Errors when days and people differ in length, when expo has a length other than 1 or the number of periods, when t has a length other than 1 or the number of periods, when prd has a length other than the number of periods, when per has more than one value, when any input has NA, Inf, text, or a value that is negative (days) or not positive (the others), and when base is not one of the two choices.

References

Lakner, E. (1976) A Manual of Statistical Sampling Methods for Corrections Planners. University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign.

See also

adp(), alos()

Examples

# Fewer people, held longer: the flow falls while the stock rises.
stkflow(
  days = c(115674, 126121), people = c(12647, 9608),
  prd = c("2023", "2025"),
  expo = c(15495050, 16256538)
)
#> ╭── Stock and flow over 2 periods ────────────────────────────────────────────╮
#> │   Periods          2023 to 2025                                             │
#> │   Period length    365 days                                                 │
#> │   Changes against  the first period                                         │
#> │   Rates per        100,000 residents                                        │
#> │   Columns          alos = days per person; adp = people held on an average  │
#> │                    day                                                      │
#> │                                                                             │
#> │   period  people     days   alos    adp  flowrate  stkrate                  │
#> │   ------  ------  -------  -----  -----  --------  -------                  │
#> │   2023    12,647  115,674   9.15  316.9     81.62    2.045                  │
#> │   2025     9,608  126,121  13.13  345.5     59.10    2.126                  │
#> │                                                                             │
#> │   2023 to 2025: people -24.0%, stay +43.5%, days +9.0%                      │
#> │   flow rate -27.6%, stock rate +3.9%                                        │
#> │   <- opposite signs: quote both, neither alone tells the story              │
#> │                                                                             │
#> │   Lakner (1976): adp = people x alos / t, exact only in a steady state.     │
#> │   A period shorter than the longest stay cuts unfinished stays short,       │
#> │   so alos is biased downward (p.16-17).                                     │
#> ╰─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

# a series of three years against the previous year, with leap-year lengths
sf <- stkflow(
  days = c(100200, 104000, 99000), people = c(9800, 9500, 9900),
  prd = 2023:2025, t = c(365, 366, 365), base = "previous"
)
as.data.frame(sf)[, c("period", "alos", "adp", "peochg", "adpchg")]
#>   period     alos      adp    peochg    adpchg
#> 1   2023 10.22449 274.5205        NA        NA
#> 2   2024 10.94737 284.1530 -3.061224  3.508829
#> 3   2025 10.00000 271.2329  4.210526 -4.546891

# days and people must line up period by period
try(stkflow(days = c(100, 120), people = c(10, 12, 14)))
#> Error : `days` and `people` must be the same length
